recovered_intent_summary: Two-site retail network. Karachi head office: 6 office PCs plus one server running an HTTP inventory system. Lahore store: 2 POS terminals that must be fully isolated (compliance), 1 back-office PC, 3 wired IP cameras on their own network, and guest WiFi for customers. Cross-site connectivity must be static routing so the inventory system is reachable from both sites; internet is required at both sites with the store on its own separate line. Exclusion: no DHCP on the POS network, POS addresses are static.
ambiguity_notes: No expected_intent is supplied, so the only requirement-bearing artifact is prompt + expected_behaviour. The three named refusal reasons cannot be derived from the prompt; they are engine-capability claims (guest-isolation-unsupported, smart_led as the only IoT kind, one internet block at sites[0]) that a reviewer cannot verify from this record.

Internal tension in expected_behaviour: reason (a) refuses the guest requirement because a 'no other device can see it' isolation guarantee is unsupported, yet the POS requirement ('koi doosra device unhe na dekh sake') is an isolation guarantee of exactly the same shape and is declared 'otherwise buildable'. If VLAN separation is enough for POS isolation, it is enough for guest internet-only; if it isn't, POS must be refused too. One of the two expectations looks wrong, or the guest refusal is really about the wireless/guest path (in which case expected_behaviour names the wrong trigger). A human should confirm.

Reason (c) sits on the boundary between a hard refusal and a planner default: 'the engine builds one internet block at sites[0]' could equally be described as a default placement that leaves the store's second line UNKNOWN rather than a reason to refuse. Refuse-vs-report-UNKNOWN is a policy choice worth confirming.

Similarly, (a) could defensibly be answered as 'build the guest VLAN, report the isolation guarantee UNKNOWN' rather than a full refusal, so the claim that there is one clearly correct response is slightly overstated.
Planner defaults (access 'dsl'-style site ids, routing mode, VLAN sizing) are not treated as inventions.
The prompt does not state the site-to-site medium for the static route, but 'connected hon' reasonably implies one and this is not load-bearing for the refusal.
human_likeness: High. Reads like a bilingual site brief a real engineer/PM would write: mixed Roman-Urdu matrix with English connectors ('so that' x2, 'and'), English technical terms (POS, DHCP, static routing, guest), headings and bullets. Only mild tell is the label 'Exclusion:', which is slightly spec/schema-flavoured signposting; 'Requirements:' is natural.
fidelity: High for the prompt itself: it states all three load-bearing facts (guest internet-only, real IP cameras required on their own wired network, store on a separate internet line) plus the POS no-DHCP/static exclusion, and no network fact is asserted that the prompt does not contain. Fidelity of the candidate as a whole depends on engine-capability claims that are unverifiable here and on the guest-vs-POS isolation tension noted above.
reason: Prompt is faithful, language-authentic and human-sounding, but the refusal expectation is internally inconsistent: it refuses the guest 'no other device can see it' guarantee while declaring the identically-shaped POS isolation guarantee buildable, and reason (c) reads as a planner default rather than a hard refusal — a human should confirm whether refusal (or build-plus-UNKNOWN) is the single correct answer.

recovered_intent_summary: One office network recently split into two VLANs; one side has six PCs and the other five. After the split about half the hosts (the five-PC side) fail DHCP, self-assign APIPA addresses and reach nothing, including the intranet server, which sits on the first VLAN and also provides DNS for the site. Rebuild the setup so both VLANs hand out proper addresses and every host that should reach the server can. Internet is DSL.
ambiguity_notes: required_hosts is 12 on both VLANs although the prompt states 6 and 5 hosts — planner sizing default, not an invention.
routing.mode 'connected' is unstated in the prompt — planner default. Likewise nat:true, public_server:false and the site id 'office' are defaults; the prompt only supplies 'DSL'.

The server's 'http' service is an inference from 'our intranet server' (the prompt only explicitly says it does DNS). Reading 'intranet server' as a web/HTTP service is reasonable, but it is an inference rather than a stated fact.

The intent delivers DHCP through VLAN-level pools (server has only http+dns), whereas the prompt's symptom (one VLAN fine, the other APIPA, DNS on the server) most often means a missing DHCP relay/ip-helper toward the server. Both fixes satisfy 'both VLANs hand out proper addresses', so this is a design choice a human might want to confirm, not a drift.
The intent places the server on the six-PC VLAN, matching the reading that 'the first VLAN' is the first-mentioned side; the split is otherwise symmetric so the mapping is not load-bearing.
No requirement about preserving the working VLAN is encoded, but rebuilding both DHCP VLANs covers it.
human_likeness: High. Natural first-person ops narrative ('We recently split our network...', 'they just self-assign', 'We're on DSL'), no signposting, no meta-text, no machine enumeration, and it states the symptom before the ask the way a network engineer would report it.
fidelity: High. Counts (6/5), the two-VLAN split, the DHCP failure with self-assignment, the server's placement on the first VLAN, its DNS role, the dual goal (DHCP on both VLANs + reachability to the server) and 'DSL' all map cleanly onto the intent; every requirement in the intent traces to a stated fact or a planner default, and nothing in the intent contradicts the prompt.
reason: Every prompt fact maps to the intent with no lost requirements and no invented network facts; the only additions (VLAN sizing, routing mode, NAT, the server's HTTP service) are planner defaults or reasonable inferences, and the English is natural with no signposting.
